newsitem.title: INDIA: India may become top world wheat producer-experts.
newsitem.headline: India may become top world wheat producer-experts.

text.p: India can surpass China and emerge as the world's largest wheat producer if productivity is raised and the area under the crop increased in the untapped eastern region, government officials and experts said on Tuesday.

"We have the scope to emerge as the world's largest wheat producer in the next ten years displacing China," R.S. Paroda director general of the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) told a seminar on wheat research in the northern town of Karnal.

Paroda said China, which annually produces about 102 million tonnes of wheat cultivates most of its crop on irrigated land and the potential to increase the yield from rain-fed areas was limited. "China has also reached a plateau as far as area under the crop is concerned."
"Our main potential lies in increasing the yield in the rain-fed areas which is currently very low," Paroda said.
Government officials said India's annual wheat demand by 2020 was expected to touch 109 million tonnes from the current 65 million tonnes.

"For this we should aim at an annual increase in production by about two million tonnes," Paroda said. "This can only be possible if upstream research is undertaken and more funds are available to develop better seeds and more effective pest control."
India harvested a record 68.7 million tonnes of wheat in 1996/97 (July-June), sharply up from 62 million tonnes in the previous year.
Officials said to meet the growing need India has to raise its average productivity level to about 3.5 tonnes per hectare from the current 2.5 tonnes.
"This is not impossible said S. Nagarajan, project director at ICAR's Directorate of Wheat Research.
Nagarajan said in some northwestern regions potential existed to raise productivity to more than 5 tonnes per hectare from the current 4.5 tonnes.
"In some northeastern regions the productivity is currently about 2.8 tonnes per hectare which could be raised to about 4.2 tonnes," Nagarajan said.
Paroda said there was a vast potential to undertake wheat cultivation in some regions in the central state of Madhya Pradesh, western state of Maharashtra and southern state of Karnataka.
He said India was currently dependent on monsoon rains for a good wheat crop.
"We need to develop wheat varieties which could prosper even if monsoon rains are not strong," Paroda said.
Experts said global demand for wheat was expected to grow sharply as preference for wheat over rice was increasing with the largest rise in demand expected from Asia.
"The preference for wheat is rising compared with rice in many countries," said H.K. Jain a former agriculture ministry official. "Major rice eating nations are gradually turning to wheat."
"When the demand is expected to grow more sharply in Asia, India cannot be complacent in finding ways to boost its production," said Paroda.
